summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would strengthen counter-terrorism powers, including frameworks for post-sentence orders and control orders, and extend their sunset dates.
It would amend the Criminal Code, Crimes Act, Surveillance Devices Act and Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Act to update and extend these powers.
The sunset date for several frameworks would be extended by 3 years to 7 December 2029.
changes: Extends the operation of control order, preventative detention order and post-sentence order frameworks for 3 years to 7 December 2029.
Extends police powers in relation to terrorism under the Crimes Act for 3 years to 7 December 2029.
Updates the high-risk terrorist offenders post-sentence order framework to reflect the increasing role of control orders.
Strengthens the control order framework to adapt to the current terrorist threat environment.
Amends provisions on de-listing terrorist organisations in the Criminal Code.
Expands protections for United Nations and associated personnel under the Criminal Code.
summary.affected: Terrorist offenders, individuals who pose a risk of committing terrorism, and agencies involved in counter-terrorism operations.

divisions.question: Milton Dick The question is that the amendments moved by the honourable member for Mayo be agreed to.

speeches.speaker: Michelle Rowland
speeches.brief: Moved the second reading of a bill extending key counter-terrorism powers to 7 December 2029 and reforming control orders, post-sentence orders, terrorist-organisation listings and protections for United Nations personnel. The bill would expand information-sharing and surveillance options, allow longer control orders for 14- to 17-year-olds, and be referred to the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security.

speeches.speaker: Tony Burke
speeches.brief: Declared that the Combatting Illicit Tobacco Bill 2026, the Australia's Foreign Relations (State and Territory Arrangements) Amendment Bill 2026, the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill 2026 and the Passenger Movement Charge Amendment Bill 2026 stand referred to the Federation Chamber for further consideration.

speeches.speaker: Julian Leeser
speeches.brief: Speaking for the Coalition, said it would not oppose the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill 2026 extending control orders and preventive detention powers to December 2029, but criticised Labor for delaying the renewal until months before expiry and for its self-managed returns policy allowing ISIS-linked women and children to return to Australia without government-controlled repatriation, citing arrests and terrorism charges laid against several returnees in 2026.

speeches.speaker: David Moncrieff
speeches.brief: Speaking in support of the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill 2026, invoked the December 2025 Bondi Beach terrorist attack that killed 15 people and Australia's 'probable' national terrorism threat level to argue for extending control order, preventive detention and post-sentence order powers to 2029, lengthening the maximum control order for radicalised young people from three to 12 months, and improving information sharing between Commonwealth and state agencies; a coalition MP said the opposition would not block the bill but criticised the government for waiting until months before the powers' sunset date to introduce it and for giving the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security insufficient time to scrutinise it.

speeches.speaker: Dean Smith
speeches.brief: Presented Scrutiny Digest 10 of 2026 of the Senate Standing Committee for the Scrutiny of Bills, covering 13 bills, and highlighted the committee's concerns about the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill 2026, including extending counterterrorism sunset powers by three years, lengthening control orders on children aged 14 to 17 from three to 12 months, and expanding surveillance powers, urging that coercive powers be issued only by judicial officers and be tightly safeguarded.

speeches.speaker: Tim Ayres
speeches.brief: Moved the second reading of the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill 2026, which would extend key counter-terrorism sunset powers by three years to 7 December 2029, make control orders the primary mechanism for managing serious terrorist offenders in place of extended supervision orders, extend the maximum control order duration for 14 to 17 year olds from three to 12 months, tighten the terrorist organisation de-listing process, and expand protections for UN personnel, citing the 2025 Bondi Beach terrorist attack that killed fifteen people.
